text: White Paper and Staff Proposal on June 22, 2022, “Advanced Strategies for Demand Flexibility Management and Customer DER Compensation.” The White Paper proposed a roadmap with a three-pillar structure of: Pillar 1, Price Presentation; Pillar 2, a 3-Prong Strategy for Rate Reform; and Pillar 3, Customer Options for Energy Optimization. The roadmap the White Paper proposed was called “CalFUSE,” or California Flexible Unified Signal for Energy, and the three pillars translated into “six key policy elements, all intended to be available on an opt-in basis”. These were: (1) provide universal access to the current electricity price through a statewide internet- based price portal that provides the current composite electricity price specific to each customer at any time (Pillar 1); (2) introduce dynamic energy prices based on real-time wholesale energy costs that reflect the localized marginal cost of energy (Pillar 2); (3) incorporate dynamic capacity prices based on real-time grid utilization (Pillar 2); (4) offer bi-directional electricity prices that allow customers to import and export energy based on the same dynamic, composite prices (Pillar 2); (5) offer a subscription option based on customer-specific load shapes (Pillar 3); and (6) enable transactive features that allow customers to lock in electricity prices to import or export a pre-determined quantity of energy at some future time (Pillar 3). The Order to Institute Rulemaking to Advance Demand Flexibility through Electric Rates (R2207005) was formally opened on July 14, 2022. The OIR noted a concern that the CPUC’s “existing piecemeal approach to load management may hinder the growth and effectiveness of demand flexibility” and decided that R2207005 would take a more systemic approach. It proposed a scope for the rulemaking of considering updates to the CPUC’s “rate design principles, guidance principles for demand flexibility, and how to streamline the patchwork of 75 niche rates and programs to expand the use of demand flexibility beyond early adopters.” In November 2022, the CPUC filed a Scoping Memo which organized the proceeding into phases, with Phase 1 having two concurrent tracks: Track A, which will “establish an income-graduated fixed charge for residential rates for all [IOUs] in accordance with [AB205] including small and multi-jurisdictional electric utilities”; and Track B, which will “streamline and expedite the adoption of demand flexibility rates” for large IOUs. Track B activities include “updating existing rate design principles for all electric rates” and “creating new demand flexibility design principles and guidance” to “establish a shared vision for demand flexibility rates.” Track B also considers “expansion of existing dynamic rate pilots as a near-term solution for supporting system reliability” for the large IOUs; consideration of “whether and how to apply Track B requirements to small and multi-jurisdictional electric utilities” was left for consideration in Phase 2.
